field_commentary.value: 鼓の滝近辺の歌枕を挙げながら、春の情景を描写している。鼓の滝は有馬山の名所で、桜の名所として平安時代から知られていた。シテの木こりが、この場所で長く過ごしている理由を説明するとき、鼓の滝の花（桜）があまりにすばらしいので、名残を惜しむ気持ちがあるためだと言う、「あり」と、「ありまやま」を掛けて、有馬山の鼓の滝と続けている。なお現在、有馬温泉近くに、鼓ヶ滝公園があり滝が流れる。そのほとりには有明桜の碑がたてられているが、かつて二本だったという有明桜そのものは今はない。

field_commentary_eng.value: By introducing the utamakura Tsuzumi no taki and its surroundings the scene evokes a spring landscape. Tsuzumi no taki is a famous place on Mount Arima, known for its cherry blossoms since the Heian period. When the woodcutter (shite) explains why he has spent so much time here, he says that the flowers (cherry blossoms) at Tsuzumi no taki are so wonderful that he regrets he has to part. The word “ari” in the sentence “hana ni nagori wa ari (mayama)” is a pivot word for “arimayama”, the sentence continuing with “arimayama no tsuzumi no taki” (Tsuzumi no taki of Arima Mountain).  Today, in the vicinity of Arima Onsen lies the Tsuzumi-ga-taki Park with this waterfall. Although there is a stele for the Ariake cherry trees near the waterfall, the two cherry trees that are said to have once stood there are no longer.

field_scene_description_eng.value:
A vassal (waki) in the service of the emperor of that time, is touring - in accordance with the imperial will to “go see the flowers of the mountains” - the flowers of various places.

This is the scene where the mountain god, disguised as a woodcutter, sings at Tsuzumi no taki (Tsuzumi waterfall) in Settsu province about the beautiful spring scenery there.

field_commentary.value:
僧（ワキ、ワキツレ）が都から芦屋へ向かう道中を謡った道行。能《忠度》の冒頭のワキ僧によるサシ「城南の離宮に赴き」から「鳴尾潟」までをそのまま借用しているので、意味は「有馬山」の《忠度》参照のこと。

ただし、《忠度》の最終目的地は須磨だが、本曲では芦屋なので、芦屋到着の謡で締める。本曲のワキ僧は本当の旅僧ではなく、執権の最明寺時頼の仮の姿であるため、心からの心象ではない。借用された謡であることは理にかなっているかもしれない。

field_commentary_eng.value: This is a michiyuki passage in the play mentioning the places some monks (waki, wakizure) pass by on their way from the capital to Ashiya.  It cites exactly the opening chant of the monk (waki) in the Nō Tadanori beginning with "sashi:  Jōnan no rikyū ni omomuki…” and ending with “Naruo gata”. (Please see for Tadanori.) The citation ends however, as the monks in the play are heading for Ashiya instead of Suma as in Tadanori. As the monk (waki) in this piece is not really a traveling monk but rather the regent Saimyōji Tokiyori in disguise, the content of the chant (hardship, floating world) does not reflect his actual feelings. We may interpret it as a borrowed chant.

field_scene_description.value:
能《藤栄》の冒頭。諸国一見の修行中の僧が、都から芦屋に向かう道中。通った歌枕を読み込んだ謡を謡って、旅をしていることを表す「道行」の場面。

ワキ僧は実は、鎌倉幕府執権の最明寺時頼（北条時頼）で、身分を僧といつわり諸国を巡見している。到着した芦屋で、領主の子月若が、叔父の藤栄に領地を横領されたことを知り、藤栄を懲らしめる。

field_scene_description_eng.value:
It is the opening scene of the Nō piece Tōei. It is about a monk who is touring the country and doing ascetic practice (shokoku ikken) and is currently on his way from the capital to Ashiya.

The michiyuki scene is expressed through a Nō chant in which the utamakura on their way are recited to indicate that the monk is on a journey.

The monk (waki) is actually Saimyōji Tokiyori (Hōjō Tokiyori), a regent of the Kamakura shogunate, disguised as a monk to travel the country. When he arrives in Ashiya, he learns that the former feudal lord’s son named Tsukiwaka has had his territory usurped by his uncle Tōei. He now goes to punish Tōei.

field_commentary.value: 僧（ワキ、ワキツレ）は「世を捨て人」つまり出家の身なので、道のりの地名によって、憂うことが多い浮き世での思い出が喚起されながら通り過ぎている。「有馬山」は摂津国有馬郡の山で、歌枕。「昆陽の池」から北西の方向にある。「憂き事の捨つる身までもあり（世を捨てた身でも憂き事はある）」の「あり」と「有馬山」の「あり」が掛詞になっている。そして、「有馬山隠れかねたる（山のように隠れがたい）」と続けて、僧になっても浮世のつらさから離れることができない、つまり忘れることができないのかと落胆しているのである。

field_commentary_eng.value: Since the monks (waki, wakitsure) are “people who have renounced the world” i.e. entered priesthood, the names of the places they pass along the way reminds them of the floating world with its many hardships. Arimayama is a mountain in Arima County, Settsu Province. It is a utamakura and is located in the northwestern direction of Koya no ike. The word “ari (exist)” in the sentence “ukikoto no sutsuru mi made mo ari” (Even those who have renounced the world lament) is a kakekotoba (a wordplay using homophonic words) to “ari” in “Arimayama”. The scene continues with “Arimayama kakurekanetaru” (As hard as it is for a mountain to hide from the world, so it is for me), which expresses his dismay that even after becoming a monk, he is unable to part from the sorrows of the floating world (i.e. he cannot forget).

field_scene_description_eng.value:
It is the opening scene of the Nō piece Tadanori. 

A monk (waki) who was a vassal of Fujiwara no Toshinari (Shunzei) and took the tonsure after Toshinari's death heads with his fellow monks (wakitsure) from the capital to the western provinces.

The michiyuki scene (the enumeration of place names and landscapes in Japanese literature, performing arts and music that illustrates a person's journey) is performed through a Nō chant reciting the utamakura on their way from the capital to Suma no ura in order to illustrate that they are on a journey. After this scene, the monks meet the spirit of Tadanori in Suma no ura.
